speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move "That the total sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The signs of this conflict had been brewing for a long time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Russian troop build-up along the Ukrainian border had taken place over many months and various NATO countries, including the US, had anticipated conflict would break out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Russia-Ukraine conflict has brought to light some concerning methods of coercion, including "false flag" operations – essentially, disinformation campaigns – to create a pretext for war.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the past year, we have witnessed other significant developments in the international security environment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, commentators have also suggested that the trajectory of the international order will be determined by developments in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a result, there is a discernible shift in the global centre of gravity and extra-regional countries are increasingly turning their attention here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes the European Union countries like the UK, France and Germany.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In one view, this is a good thing as the more invested countries are in this region, the more likely they will play a role in balancing the powers in this region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, with this growing attention focused on the Asia Pacific, we have also witnessed the emergence of new security arrangements, such as the trilateral security pact between Australia, the UK and the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The flip side of this is that there are concerns that such developments may have a divisive effect in the region or could, potentially, trigger an arms race.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another trend that has emerged is the growing intersection between geostrategic issues and technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Technology is a major area of contestation in the strategic rivalry between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Technology is also being used by both state and non-state actors that seek non-conventional ways to coerce their adversaries, including through cyber attacks and information warfare.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the pandemic has pushed us in the positive direction in terms of leveraging and maximising the use of digital platforms, this has, arguably, left our societies more susceptible to digital threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister for Defence also provide an update on how these and other geopolitical security developments are shaping MINDEF's and the SAF's plans and priorities?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How will MINDEF and the SAF respond to the challenges in our external environment and how will MINDEF and the SAF work with like-minded partners to address these threats?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, as a small nation, Singapore's security is contingent on the stability of the wider region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Because of the open and interconnected nature of Singapore's economy, major destabilising developments elsewhere can have a very tangible impact on our lives here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The ongoing battle against COVID-19 is a clear example of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Even at times when Singapore has appeared to be managing relatively well with the virus, we have seen other countries struggling.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Our dependence on trade and travel has also meant this virus would, eventually, find its way back to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The SAF has played an important role in assisting our neighbours during times of crisis, including assisting with relief efforts, when neighbours faced natural disasters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Over the years, the Minister for Defence has updated the House on MINDEF's and the SAF's efforts to cooperate with international partners to safeguard the peace and security in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, I have a question for MINDEF and the SAF and, that is, whether it is taking any steps to assist our neighbours in its battle against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Despite facing the pandemic of a century, the SAF responded admirably.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Essential operations were not suspended even during the height of the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, last year, Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen spoke about delays to major SAF programmes and initiatives due to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This would, undoubtedly, have led to an impact on SAF's medium- to long-term capability development plans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: COVID-19 has disrupted supply chains around the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Would it also disrupt the supply chains for building the next generation platforms and technologies that the SAF is seeking to acquire?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the same vein, I would also like to better understand how the pandemic has affected the SAF's ability to develop and test new training doctrines in overseas settings.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I am well aware that there are some military manoeuvres that we simply cannot practise in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And I am concerned that the COVID-19 travel restrictions over the past few years may have made it difficult for the SAF to pursue valuable training opportunities overseas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Could the Minister explain how the COVID-19 pandemic has impacted the SAF's medium- to long-term capability development plans?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic has caused huge disruptions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our SAF training has probably been one of the more heavily impacted since limited aspects of Army training can be done remotely or online.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some overseas training and exercises were affected due to travel restrictions as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that despite some disruptions, the SAF's training did not grind to a halt and that all parties managed to find ways to proceed with some exercises.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The external threats to our nation do not diminish during pandemics.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, neither should our defence preparations and training.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is happening in Europe now is a stark reminder that security threats are not pandemic-proof.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore is moving forward with our calibrated approach towards resumption of most activities, I feel that we are in a better position now than we were earlier in the pandemic, as a significant proportion of our population now is vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, our people are much more familiar with how to interact with one another safely, despite the sustained presence of the virus in our community.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, would MINDEF share an update on SAF's training at home and abroad?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Which parts of our training have returned to pre-COVID-19 levels?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, as Singapore transits to living with COVID-19, the SAF has also, gradually, resumed training for NSmen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I note that this is not without the implementation of safe management measures, testing and cohorting arrangements, to ensure the safety of our NSmen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are MINDEF's plans to recall NSmen in the coming year?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of our NSmen have not had the opportunity to participate in large-scale overseas exercises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Nations are now transiting to living with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With global borders now gradually reopening, overseas exercises must continue to be scaled up to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can MINDEF share its plans to resume larger-scale overseas exercises in 2022?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Nair, if you would like to take your two cuts together, please do.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Even as we battle COVID-19, external threats persist.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As we grapple with the pandemic and its effects, there have been new vulnerabilities for potential adversaries to exploit in order to target Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The developments in the world that I have highlighted earlier make it imperative that SAF remains operationally ready and able to function at all times, even in this pandemic environment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, now that we are one year on, I would be grateful if the Minister can provide an update on how the pandemic has affected SAF's operational readiness and whether it is still able to move into operation if necessary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Training in the SAF is an important and necessary part of our nation's defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: And as I have mentioned in my earlier cut, it is important for such training to continue even during this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, this is, in fact, the flipside of my earlier cut.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Now that SAF's training activities and operations are likely to require people to continue to work in close proximity – and these can be in camps, on ships, in military vehicles or even on exercises – there is clearly a risk of COVID-19 transmission.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I also expect that SAF will need to work on scenarios on what will happen if parts of operational units come down with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, I would be grateful if I can get an update, first of all, on what are the safety measures that are being taken to protect Servicemen in relation to COVID-19 and reduce the risk of transmission of serious illness arising from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the last two years, COVID-19 has affected virtually all aspects of our lives.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It has affected our workplaces, businesses, public offices, schools, events and many other areas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: SAF and military training have not been spared, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: SAF had to overcome the challenges which COVID-19 might have imposed on its training programmes, training methodology, restriction of travel for overseas exercise and, possibly, our morale, due to restriction of activities, including cohesion activities, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And all these without compromising SAF's combat readiness and maintaining the quality of its training regimes and programmes and the morale of our Servicemen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Both the quality and credibility of our defence force must be maintained at all times, regardless of the challenges, such as COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At last year's COS, Minister Ng Eng Hen shared with the House that despite the challenges of COVID-19, protection of key installations, maritime security, air defence and counter-terrorism efforts continue around the clock.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister also shared that COVID-19 affected some training programmes, exercises and deployments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And while certain major exercises resumed with the help of safe management measures, it might require more time to restart other exercises or for training to reach pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Minister can brief the House again on what was SAF's experience in maintaining its training regime and high-level of combat readiness last year, our second year of fighting COVID-19, and share with us the challenges which SAF had overcomed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At last year's COS, Minister Ng Eng Hen also updated the House on the involvement of many SAF personnel to assist in COVID-19-related operations for the community, such as packing masks, stabilising the outbreak in dormitories, helping to set up the community care and recovery facilities, supporting contact tracing and medical logistics operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I understand and agree with the support given by our SAF personnel in these areas, it also meant time-out from their training and their usual deployment or roles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we head towards a post-pandemic world – and this includes more countries opening up their borders – I would like to ask the Minister what are SAF's plans to work towards the resumption of training and exercises back to a pre-COVID-19 level.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will SAF be enhancing training for all our forces and Servicemen and, in a sense, making up for their time spent away from our training or operational role as a result of COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and, with it, a new world order, is unfolding before our very eyes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are many lessons that we can draw from the new reality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A strong SAF is vital in deterring potential aggressors and in protecting Singapore's peace and stability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We cannot expect others to shed blood for us.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, we must work hard to build the Next-Generation SAF and stay ahead of rapidly changing defence and warfare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, with the rapid evolution of technology, interstate conflict may no longer manifest in conventional physical or kinetic modes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Conflict could instead be conducted through grey zone tactics below the threshold of war, or through attacks in the cyber and digital domains, where most of us now live and work following the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And even as the domains and modalities for conflict continue to expand and grow, existing threats to our peace and security, such as terrorism, remain salient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also recognise the importance of SAF ensuring that its platforms and capabilities serve as a credible deterrent to conventional military threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, any perceived weak point in our military capabilities is a vulnerability that could be exploited and the SAF must remain ready and prepared to respond to the ever-growing range of challenges to defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I welcome the efforts to build the Next-Generation SAF, as MINDEF and SAF first announced in 2019.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is timely and necessary that SAF harnesses technology to respond better to security threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Mr Chairman, our low birth rate is a significant challenge to Singapore's defence strategy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: At the same time, new technologies have allowed us to better optimise manpower resources and complete tasks better, more efficiently and with less manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I believe that MINDEF and SAF have already made strides in this area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: For example, at last year's COS, the Minister for Defence spoke about the inauguration of the Singapore Army's Headquarters Sense & Strike (HQ SS), which integrated various technology-enabled capabilities, to allow the Army to "see better and shoot faster" with less manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The Minister also spoke about how new technology had enabled SAF to redesign more jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: SAF can then tap on a larger pool of Servicemen to serve in roles that they would have previously been ineligible for under SAF's old medical classification system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This included being deployed to protect key installations, now augmented by unmanned watch towers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: SAF has been working closely with the defence technology community to leverage advances in technology to better support the needs of our defence strategies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The use of technology, such as drones, can significantly make up for a shortfall in personnel.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The ongoing hostility in Ukraine is difficult to ignore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The onslaught of cyber attacks that the Ukrainian government is facing shines a light on the nature of warfare in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Battles are fought not just in the sea, air and on land, but also in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Ukraine is not alone when facing such threats.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Recent events have underscored that these attacks can be initiated by non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Major ransomware attacks have targeted critical infrastructure in different parts of the world, causing serious, real-world disruptions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: In fact, Singapore has experienced such cyber attacks as well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: In the years ahead, it seems likely that potential cyber attacks will continue to increase in frequency, scale and complexity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: If these attacks were to successfully target our military infrastructure and systems, there would be dire consequences.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: In the light of this, could the Minister for Defence provide views on how threats in the digital domain are evolving and what MINDEF and SAF are doing to better address these evolving threats?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The cybersecurity threat landscape is constantly evolving in the current digital age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These threats, which include ransomware, denial-of-service attacks and advanced persistent threats, are originating further up the value chain by impacting operational technology and threatening critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As a result, the effects of cybersecurity threats have left no stone unturned, as it has the potential to adversely impact governmental operations, global supply chains, healthcare systems and our military systems, among others.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On the defence and national security front, we have seen the increased prevalence of grey zone operations involving malicious cyber campaigns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At last year’s Committee of Supply, the Minister for Defence said that the Cybersecurity Task Force had been stood up, as part of SAF’s plans to monitor and actively seek out potential threats and aggressors in the cyber domain.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think this is a step in the right direction to shore up Singapore’s defences in the digital domain.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In view of this, I would like to ask the Minister for Defence for an update on the SAF’s ongoing efforts to enhance our military’s cybersecurity to address these emerging cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, the rise of China and the evolving geopolitical situation between China and the US had a global impact, especially on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When US President Richard Nixon visited China 50 years ago in 1972, the US was a superpower while China was seen as the sick man of Asia.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In terms of nominal GDP, the size of China's economy in 1972 was just 8.9% of the US economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But in 2020, China's economy became 70.3% of the US economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is projected that China's economy will overtake the US economy by 2030.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The rivalry between the two countries has given rise to stiff competition in technology, innovation and defence build-up.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As a result, Quad and AUKUS were formed to counter the influence of China.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many ASEAN countries, including Singapore, have been asked to take sides.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We are being swept up in this current of geopolitical change.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Will Singapore continue to welcome US nuclear submarines at our naval base and, eventually, host Australia's nuclear submarine when New Zealand had categorically said no?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In view of the COVID-19 pandemic, especially the latest Omicron wave, how does it affect MINDEF's engagement with its US and Chinese counterparts, including the joint exercises with these two countries respectively?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Has the ongoing Ukraine war affected our defence relations with the US and China?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, as a small state, Singapore’s defence depends not only on our will and ability to defend ourselves, but also the strategic friendships that we maintain with other nations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore is particularly vulnerable to shocks that take place in our external environment, often due to developments outside of our control.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, our cooperation with like-minded partners in areas of common interest is important.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the world looks to step out of the COVID-19 shadow, I am glad to see that diplomatic meetings and engagements are starting to return.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I imagine that virtual formats may not be the most conducive means to build mutual trust.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding that, I am sure that MINDEF and SAF have innovated new ways to keep up international engagements and advance partnerships in extraordinary times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How are MINDEF and SAF cooperating with their foreign counterparts to address common security challenges?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also important to note that national security threats have evolved today and may now take less conventional forms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead of hot war or armed conflict, different threats, such as cyber attacks, hostile information campaigns and even future pandemics, might endanger our lives and livelihoods, equally or even to a greater extent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In view of that, what are the principles guiding our defence diplomacy efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will we see more agreements to conduct joint military exercises and our SAF training abroad, or for other types of cooperation like the cybersecurity MOU we signed with the US Department of Defence when US Vice President Kamala Harris visited Singapore last year?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to ask MINDEF about the implications of the Defence Cooperation Agreement with Indonesia for Singapore and for SAF.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The Prime Minister recently visited Indonesia for the Singapore-Indonesia Leaders’ Retreat hosted by Indonesian President Jokowi.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I am heartened by the good progress that we have made in advancing our bilateral interests in issues, such as the Flight Information Region, extradition and military training, especially following the long-drawn discussions and negotiations on these issues, which started back in 1995.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What does the DCA with Indonesia mean for Singapore, MINDEF and SAF?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The recent crisis in Ukraine has thrown up stark reminders to all nation-states, big or small, that cooperation in times of need is critical.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Globally, US-China tensions have polarised countries, both in our region and further afield.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These have manifested in various geopolitical theatres, including the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Internally, many ASEAN countries are facing challenges domestically, economically and with the current pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A region that is divided and distracted is not in our interest.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore should seek to facilitate stronger cooperation among ASEAN countries, given the increasingly complex regional landscape.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ADMM prides itself as being open and inclusive in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister for Defence provide an update on MINDEF's efforts to foster greater cooperation through ADMM?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ADMM and ADMM-Plus are the region's security architecture and are meant to contribute to regional peace and stability among all 18 countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the developments in Ukraine, what is the impact on the work and security cooperation of both ADMM and ADMM-Plus?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Chairman, climate change poses an existential threat to all humanity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: The related crises arising from climate change have deep implications for international peace and stability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Singapore is one of the more vulnerable nations due to the rising sea level.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: We are already experiencing erratic weather patterns which wreak havoc with sudden downpours causing flooding.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Changes in weather patterns are also affecting food supplies – a frightening prospect, as we rely heavily on imported food; exporting nations will prioritise their own nations’ needs first.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: While Singapore may be limited in how we can contribute to global climate action, we should spare no effort as we have a strong moral obligation and duty.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Would the Ministry share an update on its measures to improve environmental sustainability and reduce carbon emissions within SAF and MINDEF?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: I urge the Ministry to continue with its systematic and comprehensive approach to sustainability, from reducing food waste to trying out green aviation fuel for RSAF’s fighter jets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: I look forward to hearing more about its green initiatives, improved processes and enhanced inspections to prevent wastage, particularly for food and electricity.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, thank you for allowing me to reply to the Members' cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I will try to answer as many of the questions that they have asked.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The others will be replied to by the Senior Ministers of State.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, I state the obvious when I say that battling COVID-19 has been the central preoccupation of governments and their citizens all over the world in the last two years, including Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If we think about it, very few events have that power and reach.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In recent history, I think World War II did, and that shared experience had defined that affected generation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you compare, COVID-19 is not as devastating as World War II, but many years on, I suspect that it will likely linger in the memories of all those who have lived through it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But despite the singular challenge of this century, COVID-19, there is no respite, no temporary cessation of other challenges that pose security threats to Singapore, as some Members have observed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: My Ministry and SAF have remained very focused on the security environment even as we went into the trenches to join the whole-of-Government in our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF’s core purpose, first and foremost, must remain to protect Singapore from all potential external aggressors.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Vikram Nair alluded to this, Mr Dennis Tan, too.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And because we are a small country, with less space figuratively and literally to react, we need to recognise these threats early.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Singapore’s survival and well-being, the SAF not only needs to be always prepared, to plan long term and be well-organised, but also nimble to change, if we are to prevent or ward off imminent danger.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Therefore, despite our efforts to fight COVID-19, MINDEF and SAF have continued to plan in earnest so that we build the next generation SAF that is not only capable of meeting today’s security threats, but anticipating tomorrow’s, too.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And I think that must be our approach.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There will always be the unexpected threats, just like COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But the better the SAF is structured to deal with the known threats, the more bandwidth it has to deal with the unknown unknowns.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I will deal with some of these initiatives later on, which Members have asked for.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But, first, let me put MINDEF’s budget this year in context.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I should underscore that we continued to purchase and acquire new platforms despite COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For example, deliveries of RSAF’s H225M Medium Lift and CH-47F Heavy Lift helicopters were delayed from end-2020 to March and May 2021, respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The delivery of our Invincible-class submarines, initially planned for last year, has also been delayed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For this year and beyond, projects deferred or delayed will resume, as will the acquisition of new platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have asked about training – Mr Don Wee, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Shawn Huang.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF expects to increase numbers of training, both locally and overseas, to reach pre-COVID-19 levels later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Last year, we, indeed, had fewer overseas exercises and with fewer troops.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For example, Exercise Forging Sabre in the US, with 800 personnel, Exercise Wallaby in Australia with around 580 personnel, much fewer than pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At home, NS training has progressively returned to normalcy and in-camp training call-up rates are on track to reach pre-COVID-19 levels this year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The reduction in spending over the last two years did not occur at the expense of readiness.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have asked about this – Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, SAF was able to operate at a high level of readiness and conduct critical operations amidst the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Soldiers within units were disciplined and kept to strict health and safety protocols, such as health screening for all recruits and instructors, training in smaller groups where possible, temperature taking, testing, and testing returning NSmen from their In-Camp Trainings (ICTs) every seven days.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And that has helped us keep our infections at bay.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I said that we were determined to keep building up the next-generation SAF – Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Desmond Choo asked for updates.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Formidable-class frigates, first commissioned in 2007, are now 15 years old and due for their midlife upgrade.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They are our key fighting platforms for maritime strike, anti-air and anti-submarine warfare, but the midlife upgrade, as we do for all platforms, will be more than just addition and alterations, if I can use the construction term.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The next-generation SAF, which Mr Desmond Choo asked about, too, will have more unmanned systems across the three services.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are among the first few navies in the world to operate unmanned maritime systems.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These systems were designed and integrated locally by DSO National Laboratories and Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) and RSN.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are immensely proud of and grateful for the men and women of DSO, who, for the past five decades, have worked hard behind-the-scenes to provide game-changing defence technologies and solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They have transformed the SAF into today's modern fighting machine.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members would remember that at last year's Committee of Supply (COS), I spoke about the inauguration of the Headquarters Sense and Strike (HQ SS) and the HQ SS was able to participate for the first time in exercise Forging Sabre late last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can already see its new form now, inchoate, but with greater definition as each year passes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This next-generation SAF will provide for this and the next generation, our children and theirs, greater confidence in dealing with potential aggressors to fulfil the SAF's core mission.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many Members have asked how we navigate the increasingly complex geopolitical situation and rivalries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am afraid no country has a magic formula, no Aladdin's lamp that you can make wishes from.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We make friends with all countries and seek no enemies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we are realists, too, and keen observers of history and events around us, and, especially what happens to small, vulnerable states.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We saw how Kuwait, an oil-rich state, was invaded by Iraq in 1990.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We observed how Qatar suffered an air, land and sea blockade imposed by its neighbours in 2017, not so long ago.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And at this very moment, we witness Ukrainians deeply troubled as they ponder over their future, balanced on a knife's edge.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Their cities are under bombardment and with foreign troops; their way of life, their dreams are shattered; their independence and freedom are under peril.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ukraine, with a population of over 40 million, is not a small country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For them, Kuwaitis and Qataris, these moments are about life and death, freedom or subjugation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Indeed, we live by the dictum that the stronger the SAF, the easier it is to make friends and have fewer enemies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: No one will defend Singapore as robustly if Singaporeans do not or cannot.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if we are able to build up the kind of SAF by 2040, can we be satisfied collectively, as leaders in the Government and Members of this House, that we have discharged our duties honourably and with satisfaction to our children's generation?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some here might say, yes, because that kind of SAF is impressive.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think our founding fathers could not have envisaged that we could have come quite this far.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will, certainly, be among the most modern and better-equipped militaries in the region.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But my honest answer is "almost there, but not quite", because, as good and as ambitious as the next-generation SAF is, there are some gaps in capabilities, which recent events and developments have warned us against.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I am glad that Members of this House have warned us, too – Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I am talking primarily about threats in the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will spend some time elaborating on this significant move as the reasons are important.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Let us characterise the digital threat, first, in broad general terms, to know what countries, including Singapore, are up against.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The digital terrain has become as real as the land, air and sea domains for which we have raised the Army, Air Force and Navy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, some would argue that, for the next generations, the digital domain is the dominant domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So much so that a new word "metaverse" has been coined for that virtual universe.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Threats that emanate in the digital domain can readily impact events in a real physical world.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That divide between virtual and physical, in security terms, is a false one as the two are, in fact, intricately interwoven.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There have also been clear examples of countries or non-state entities, like terrorist groups, that use a combination of attacks through both the digital and physical domains.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I first spoke about this type of hybrid warfare seven years ago in my 2015 COS speech, but, over the past few years, there have been many more examples of this type of campaigns.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even now, we are witnessing with our own eyes that kind of campaign in Ukraine.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Financial Times reported it, with the headline: "Ukraine shores up cyber defences" and this was on 14 February, so quite recent.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Ukraine government and independent experts expect hostile cyber activity to increase, in an effort to destabilise the country before or during any physical attack".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Another quote: "There are bound to have been many, many more attacks over the years that we do not know about and that have left malware embedded in systems ready to be activated" – this was a quote from Prof VS Subrahmaniam, who is a professor of Computer Science at Northwestern University in the US.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He adds: "It is a bit like a bomb being planted in your house, is benign until someone sets it off".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Another quote: "Ukraine meanwhile suffers from a deficit of public sector cyber security expertise, weak regulation, limited response capabilities and a lack of coordination between various agencies".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think all of the Members would agree with me here that we can learn from this unfortunate situation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And far better to learn and adjust now, because if we wait and change only after an attack on ourselves, the cost is going to be very high.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When we look at all these incidents in the digital domain, what then should our response be?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Fortunately, our intelligence sources have not identified such orchestrated attempts to subvert or subjugate Singapore using hybrid means.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, of course, that does not mean that the threat will never come.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I think, we best prepare now with a longer runway.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And for SAF, a clear-cut response is a fourth service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Internally, over the past decade, MINDEF/SAF have progressively built up what we call the C4I – Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And some of you have asked for updates, even at this COS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The C4I community and its predecessors, the Military Intelligence Organisation and Joint C4, have been supporting elements to the three other services for over 20 years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, the demands and direct responsibilities on the intelligence community for both threats in the digital and physical world have risen sharply.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If we take terrorism, for example, the role of the C4I community is not only supportive but a direct responsibility.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members would remember that when 9/11 occurred, it was characterised as a failure in intelligence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Shortly thereafter, Members might recall that decisive actions by ISD, based on good intelligence, foiled a Jemaah Islamiyah plot to launch terrorist attacks in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The formation of a new service for the C4I community will greatly facilitate their mission focus, sharpen direct responsibility and accountability, and capability development.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The human resource is particularly important for the intelligence services and having a Service status, just like Army, Navy and Air Force, will enhance recruitment and career prospects considerably.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The evolution of the C4I community into a new fourth service will integrate and expand our capabilities in the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we will need more than that to deal effectively with digital threats from external aggressors that we expect will grow in number, sophistication and organisation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To achieve this, we will need not only an intelligence force but a dedicated digital force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The current DCO is building up such a force but it is insufficient for the SAF’s expanding needs and mandate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF and SAF have been considering these changes for some time now, exploring various options to better prepare for threats in the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: DIS should not and cannot be just like the Army, Air Force and Navy, with similar troops operating in the digital domain instead of the physical domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The nature of the digital domain and the threats therein require different skillsets, mindsets – what we call Tactics, Techniques and Procedures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF envisages that the type of soldiers you recruit for DIS, their training, force structure will be different.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But some traits must be maintained for soldiers across the four services – the adherence to SAF core values, operational mindset, resilience that lead to mission success and, above all, a commitment to the shared mission to enhance Singapore’s security and peace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Technology, especially related to IT and communications, will play a big role for DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it will also require a force with specialisations not only in core IT areas and communications, but in diverse areas, including data science, psychology, linguistics, anthropology and geography, that will help them understand the motivation and means by which orchestrated state and non-state groups aim to harm Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The addition of this fourth service, the DIS, will allow SAF to better train and fight as a networked, integrated and expanded force to deal with the spectrum of threats that we know exist today, but also the digital domain that we know will increase in the future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Other countries have also come to the same conclusion and added a digital force to their tri-services.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There are many procedures and processes to undertake to set up this fourth service, DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: NSmen form the backbone of the SAF, on land, air and sea and, in the future, also our digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Whatever our plans, ultimately, it is the quality and commitment of our NSmen that will determine whether SAF can succeed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This year marks the 55th anniversary of NS and, as we have previously done, we will have a number of events to recognise their contributions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will put out more details in the coming months.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we also want to make improvements to our NS system.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These new initiatives are from the NS Review Committee, which some Members have asked about, which is chaired by the Deputy Secretary (Administration) of MINDEF and the Chief of Army.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman asked about this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Compared to general physical assessments, functional assessments are a more precise gauge of whether the Servicemen can perform specific vocations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the same time, we have redesigned 1,000 jobs so that more Servicemen can contribute in areas they were not previously eligible for.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There will be a default base NS pay which NSmen can claim for In-Camp Training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This will be especially useful for those in informal employment and training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How will provide more details on these changes, as well as several others.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This four-service Next Gen SAF, with committed and capable NSmen, will better position Singapore to deal with both conventional and emerging threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our deterrence depends on a strong Next Gen SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But another prong is good relations, which many Members have talked about, particularly defence relations, with like-minded partners.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about our approach.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a small country, Singapore needs as many friends as we can have.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Having a strong network of defence partners has allowed us to build up our defence capabilities, train overseas and cooperate on strategic issues critical to our security.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the past year, we maintained high-level defence engagements.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, US Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin made his introductory visit to Singapore in July and we concluded a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) Concerning Cooperation in Cyberspace with the US Department of Defense in August.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: With China, I met Minister for National Defense General Wei Fenghe virtually in June.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The RSN held joint naval exercises with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army via a “contactless” modality twice last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: With India, we signed an MOU in January for the SAF to conduct weapon firings in India’s Chandipur Integrated Test Range.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We renewed the Singapore-Vietnam Defence Cooperation Agreement in February.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have also concluded new defence cooperation agreements with a few Baltic States, to institutionalise our professional exchanges.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We decided that the Baltic States were of interest and this happened before Ukraine.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I think that cooperation will bear more fruit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Closer to home, we conducted Exercise Safkar Indopura with the Indonesian Army in November, the first physical exercise between our Army and a foreign counterpart.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked what the implication of this is.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The DCA will strengthen the strategic relationship between our defence establishments and promote closer interaction and cooperation between our armed forces.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about our approach to ADMM-Plus and ADMM.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is, indeed, the de facto multilateral defence grouping in Asia, and we have taken the lead on tackling threats in the cyber and information domains by establishing the ADMM Cybersecurity and Information Centre of Excellence, which now provides monthly reports for all ASEAN Member States.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similarly, SAF’s Counter Terrorism Information Facility (CTIF) has been in operation since 2020 and 11 foreign liaison officers are stationed there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The CTIF produces timely and actionable counter-terrorism intelligence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am also pleased that, this year, the Shangri-La Dialogue will resume in June physically, after a two-year hiatus.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Chairman, let me also update Members on MINDEF/SAF’s major green initiatives, which Mr Don Wee has asked about, which I announced at the last COS, to reduce the growth of overall emissions by two-thirds by 2030.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF Sustainability Office, led by SAF’s Chief of Staff-Joint Staff, has convened an external panel comprising experts to provide insights on implementation plans to meet our sustainability targets.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members have asked for updates, let me give some.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: By the end of this year, about a quarter of SAF camps will have solar panels installed to deliver 20 megawatt peak of electricity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is equivalent to the consumption of around 5,000 4-room households.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: By 2025, it will jump from a quarter to two-thirds of our camps generating 50 megawatt peak of electricity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Smart Metering Systems will also be installed to track electricity and water consumption automatically, starting with Jurong Camp, Paya Lebar Airbase and Changi Naval Base.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: RSAF has commenced trials for the use of green fuel for its F-16 Fighting Falcons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These efforts and others will help us meet our emission targets by 2030.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am thankful that Members of this House have supported our budget each year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On MINDEF and SAF’s part, our responsibility is to spend prudently and effectively to build a strong national defence, as I have detailed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it is gratifying to me, and to Members here, too, that SAF is a national asset to deploy in situations like the current COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our defence scientists and engineers contributed a variety of support systems.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we were pleasantly pleased that others were saying the right things on behalf of MINDEF and SAF, and of their own convictions, of course.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I think salutary lessons have sunk in and, indeed, some Singaporeans have sent me emails.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: One is from Mr Tee KH: “I used to take my in-camp training as a ‘holiday’ camp till I realised how important it is to defend Singapore when Iraq invaded tiny Kuwait.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Now a retiree and from the Merdeka Generation, I reminded my son who is serving NS to take his training seriously.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The greater the force of dutiful citizens who are actively serving their country, defending the weak, fighting for freedom and doing what is right, the better chance that wars will end quickly and the less chance wars will even begin.” The second is from Mr Cheng CF: “If Singaporeans don’t defend our country, nobody will help us.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, the Minister for Defence mentioned that the new system will also take into account the civilians' jobs and skill sets.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The review of the medical classification system is a step in the right direction, as MINDEF aims to optimise its human resources amidst dwindling birth rates in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The review would be helpful in enabling the SAF to assess individual abilities for suitable vocations holistically.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Could MINDEF provide an update on this new medical classification system?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Specifically, can MINDEF elaborate on how have individuals been assessed and how MINDEF has ensured that the assessment remains holistic for vocation matching?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I was subsequently posted to a maintenance battalion, to be converted to an ordnance officer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It was an odd move because I was a Junior College (JC) Arts student majoring in history, geography and economics, with no technical background.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But during my National Service, I had to learn about how hydraulics can move a tank turret, how to maintain a 75-millimetre gun in the tank, how to overhaul a car engine and how to replace a clutch disk.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: On the other hand, some of my friends who are Polytechnic graduates in mechanical engineering, were posted to be storemen.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Nothing wrong with these vocations, Sir, but it seems just a mismatch of skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The skillsets which some of my JC and Polytechnic friends had were not optimised during their National Service.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, I was pleased to hear about MINDEF's plans to optimise the deployment of its NSmen.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I thought it was a move in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Technology has changed the way soldiers can be deployed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Heng Chee How mentioned about the trial functional assessments to guide the selection of transport operators.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Are there plans to expand functional assessments to other vocations, so that our NSmen can be better deployed and they will feel that their time spent during NS has been meaningful and useful?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, the pandemic has disrupted our economy and our way of life and in particular, greatly affected the education, training and learning opportunities for our youths.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the last two years, many of these programmes and lessons had to be shifted online.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While this arrangement has been necessary, our youths have missed out on valuable in-person interactions and hands-on experiences.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Through these disruptions, the economy has developed unevenly and the job market is full of uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our primary responsibility is to train and develop our NSFs to undertake their missions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, it is also important that we help to prepare and equip them to enter the workforce as best as we can.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last year, it was announced that the first batch of NSF technicians from the Army and Air Force were being trained and certified under this programme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the Work-Learn Scheme?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many servicemen have benefited from the scheme since it was launched?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there any future plans to expand this scheme?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, there are many of us in this House who have once upon a time donned uniforms and held guns.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Two years' fulltime, during my time, it was two and a half years, and many years after that, serving our country in the Armed Forces.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have all had friends who have different specialist skills and expertise, but for weeks on end, they will leave their professions and their expert knowledge behind to go to serve during our reservist call-ups as Operationally-Ready NSmen.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It also has a dedicated deployment centre to oversee the expansion of expertise deployment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Professionals, such as those working in cybersecurity, law, medicine, engineering and psychology, have been deployed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In a small country, facing many complex threats and risks, such deployment offers us a good way to maximise the men and women who are serving our country.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister tell us how MINDEF/SAF is exploring ways to better leverage the civilian expertise of our National Servicemen to meet the operational needs of the SAF?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Overall, can the Minister give us an idea of the expertise-based deployment scheme?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How many experts have signed up and in what areas?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How do their deployments differ from the usual deployments and have they been able to make an impact?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given the fact that the scheme is fairly new, what lessons have we learnt and how do we compare against citizen armed forces in other countries?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, digital technology has evolved exponentially in the last decade.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It has changed the way people and organisations interact and exchange information and transact.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The pandemic has accelerated this trend as people and organisations seek ways to minimise physical contact.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Digital payment has been well and widely adopted in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: From small shops to large businesses and person-to-person transactions, digital payment is now the norm and this trend will continue to pick up pace.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: MINDEF and SAF should leverage more on technology and digitalisation to improve the way servicemen transact and interact.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Digital services can help to streamline many administrative processes and reduce waiting time for our servicemen and pre-enlistees.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: A large proportion of our servicemen are young NSFs who are digital natives and comfortable with performing tasks online.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, National Service is an irreplaceable component for our nation's defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: All men in Singapore commit two years of their youth to safeguard our country as full-time NSmen or NSFs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They set aside work and family obligations, at times, life milestones during their years as reservists.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is important that we ensure that NSmen and their families receive support and are recognised for their sacrifices.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the case of 2020 NS Advocate Award Winner, Mdm Nur Kamilah binte Abdul Rahman, we saw the sacrifice of a wife and mother who chose to find alternatives to nurse a sick child and still care for another while her husband was on reservist, despite his insistence on returning home earlier.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Her story is just one of the many sacrifices NSmen and their families have made.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We also recognise and are grateful that much has been done over the years to honour our NSmen.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With a changing societal landscape, it is timely for us to review the recognition for our NSmen, not only by MINDEF, but also how the whole of society, including our employers, can better support our NSmen.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged that this was identified as a priority area and would like to ask how can the Government better recognise and support not only our NSFs, but also the NSmen in the SAF and Home Team who have completed their full-time National Service.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How can we encourage our employers to better support our NSmen?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, for the past 55 years, NSmen have been a pillar of Singapore's defence – in fact, a key pillar.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is important for us not to take our NSmen's contributions to our nation's security for granted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Instead, we should seek to recognise their contributions, and work continually to improve the NS system so that every National Serviceman has a fulfilling and meaningful NS experience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Members before me have welcomed the formation of the NS Review Committee (NSRC) in 2020 which seeks to examine ways to enrich the NS experience and maximise the potential of every National Serviceman.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I echo these words of support and look forward to hearing MINDEF's updates on what changes are being made.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond this, could MINDEF please provide an update on the Committee's recommendations on future areas for review within the NS system?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Only when our soldiers are competent, can they fight effectively and achieve their mission to be a strong deterrent to unfriendly forces.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The war in Ukraine is a stark reminder on the need for realistic training and the importance of National Service.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But even as soldiers train under tough conditions, it is vital that they train safely.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: A strong commitment to training safety will give our soldiers the confidence to focus on honing their skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It will give parents and family members of our servicemen peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Without these, there would not be strong public support for defence and National Service.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: As much as training safety continues to be an area of emphasis, the nature of military activities will always entail some risk of injury.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: How do we ensure that our servicemen are adequately protected when they perform their NS duties and what are some of the recent efforts to enhance safety management in the SAF?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: How do we ensure that our commanders take training safety seriously and put it as their priority that no NSmen under their command will suffer any serious injury?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, safety is not something that should gain salience only when incidents occur.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must always keep safety at the forefront of our minds.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The SAF must ensure that our servicemen and women return home to their families safe and sound.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They should be kept safe not only in terms of their physical but mental health, too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This panel, like the panels before them, comprises a diverse range of experts who are well-positioned to provide fresh perspectives to the SAF.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How are these efforts being translated into positive outcomes to strengthen SAF's safety culture?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For families who have sent their children to serve National Service, they must be assured of safe training.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For SAF, its safety record reflects well on how our troops and resources are managed.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support efforts to critically review how the SAF's Services and Formations implement safety policies and assess the strength and prevalence of the safety culture.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Of course, the defence industry or ecosystem is no exception.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Militaries around the world have been leveraging on technology to transform themselves.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The possibilities range from enhancements in systems efficiency to augmented reality-based immersive training experiences.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: My focus today, however, is something closer to our hearts – the safety of our servicemen and women.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The proliferation of tools to harness data could aid the development of training regimes that are more effective, more efficient and most importantly, safe.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The concept of Total Defence has taken on a different complexion since it was first introduced in 1984 in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Back then, Total Defence was a national defence concept that rallies all Singaporeans behind the Singapore Armed Forces should there be a military threat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, Total Defence has evolved and included non-military challenges, such as pandemics, economic recessions and natural disasters.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has tested Singapore's resilience and unity heavily.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans now not only have to put up a strong psychological defence in overcoming mental wellness and safety management changes in their daily lives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Economically, supply chain disruptions have affected the access and affordability of essential goods for many.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Civil defence was at play too in the introduction of contact tracing and safety management measures.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, other aspects of Total Defence have come into play, such as digital defence, as Singapore becomes more exposed to cybersecurity risks in a highly-wired society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is also the continued need to emphasise the importance of military defence, especially in the wake of developments as recent as the Russian-Ukraine war.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst many Singaporeans are fairly familiar with six pillars of Total Defence – namely, Military, Civil, Economic, Social, Digital and Psychological – not many are aware of exactly how important and relevant each of the pillars is and how each pillar of defence is manifested in the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the light of Budget 2022, how would resources be differently applied in this regard?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, one key demographic for outreach efforts on defence and security issues is our younger generation of Singaporeans here.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Unlike our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations, our youth today and perhaps even their parents, have not had direct experiences of the Singapore in which insecurity and physical intimidation by external threats were a daily reality.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: As the future leaders of Singapore, it is important that young people are engaged and understand defence and security issues to gain an appreciation of the potential threats we face, as well as how these issues affect their lives and the lives of their families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Many security threats are now more ambiguous, less tangible and more difficult to understand.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: This may further disconnect defence issues from the day-to-day concerns of young people, especially having grown up in the context of a prospering Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Our youths have also grown up more socially aware than those of earlier generations, and that is something to celebrate.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: At the same time, this also means there is an exposure to worldviews that may potentially fuel divides in civil society where worldviews may be applied without an in-depth understanding of the socio-historical background and its larger impact on Singapore society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Singapore's defence requires not only the effort and the work of MINDEF and the SAF, but the support and involvement of every man and woman in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: For some, defence and security matters may seem abstract, but the reality is that all of our lives would be impacted if Singapore's sovereignty and security were undermined.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The war in Ukraine is also a stark reminder of the ongoing need to be ready to defend our sovereignty and not to take it for granted.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: It is thus critical that Singaporeans of all ages see the importance of defence issues and understand the role that each and every person plays in national defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: In light of this, I believe that it is important for MINDEF and the SAF to make a conscious effort to engage Singaporeans in every demographic, from all walks of life and encourage them to learn and care about defence issues, especially during peace time.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Last year, Senior Minister of State for Defence Zaqy Mohamad spoke about MINDEF's efforts to develop creative ways to engage Singaporeans on defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: An example is the revamped Singapore Discovery Centre.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: He also shared that MINDEF will take on public suggestions to empower more Singaporeans to learn about defence issues.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, the Singapore Discovery Centre (SDC) is one of the venues built by the Government to present National Education in an interesting and engaging way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Here, visitors learn and experience Singapore's history and visualise its future in a fun and immersive way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: One of the main objectives of the centre is to help build a strong sense of belonging and identity among Singaporean visitors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: As a young nation, it is critical that Singaporeans understand our history, what brought us together and who we are as one people.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In this regard, our National Education is what enables Singaporeans to imbibe, understand and connect with what it means to be a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: An important part of being Singaporean is our commitment and ability to defend our land and our way of life.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is important that Singaporeans, young and old, understand the importance of National Service and Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: NS and Total Defence require all Singaporeans to step up to defend and protect our home and rally behind our soldiers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Last year, Senior Minister of State for Defence Zaqy Mohamad announced that the SDC would be revamped to be a one-stop destination for learning about Singapore’s past and imagining its future.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the heart of national defence is the amicable community relations Singaporean families have with our military.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the thick of the pandemic, military units continued to honour their departing Servicemen in milestone parades, making sure to arrange for remote viewing avenues such that Singaporean families could share in the pride and joy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, MINDEF and the Armed Forces’ have signalled their holistic commitment to the defence of Singapore in our greatest times of testing, mobilising our Servicemen to aid in contact tracing measures which are pivotal as we deal with COVID-19 as a nation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we enjoy such relations, MINDEF has and continues to regularly consult and partner grassroots and agencies to take pulse checks on Singaporeans’ outlook on defence issues, as well as to foster support for their various initiatives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that Singapore’s defence is a nationally-owned effort, it is important for ACCORD to continue to reach out to groups and individuals in key segments of society – the business sector, educational institutions and family-related bodies – to mobilise support for and foster better understanding of our defence issues, including NS.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These channels are valuable for MINDEF to better listen to the community’s needs and interests and, therefore, shape messages and tailor programmes to engage different sectors and profiles within the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could MINDEF please update the House on ACCORD’s new initiatives and future plans to engage the community?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can ACCORD furnish us with more details about consultation efforts with the grassroots on Singapore’s defence issues and how Singaporeans wish to get engaged?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is an honour to serve alongside other Members to promote the support for NS amongst families and employers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ours is an important role because NS is key to our concept of Total Defence, which covers not just military defence preparedness but also fosters greater identity and social cohesion amongst our young men in NS, who come from all races, religions and backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A resolute defence comprises two things: first, a credible and strong SAF and, second, the unshakeable resolve of our people.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NS provides the opportunity for Singaporeans to forge a deep sense of rootedness and resolve to defend what is ours and our way of life.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A strong SAF, augmented by NS, serves as a strong deterrent, which goes hand-in-hand with diplomacy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NS has served us well, and long may it continue.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we do more to involve all Singaporeans in our defence, including employers, parents of new citizens or those who wish to pursue sports or further education and, thus, seeking deferment of NS?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Chairman, Defence Minister Dr Ng Eng Hen spoke yesterday about the challenging landscape in which the SAF would have to operate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our National Servicemen form the bulk of our defence and security force, and NS is the bedrock of our national defence, giving us that firm foundation for Singapore’s survival, security and success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For the past 55 years, generations of Singaporean males have served their country through NS and had done their duty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As we commemorate 55 years of NS this year, it is timely for us to reaffirm our commitment towards ensuring that our NS system remains relevant to the needs of the SAF in protecting our country and is relevant to our National Servicemen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Minister Ng Eng Hen outlined the key changes arising from the NS Review Committee, or NSRC’s work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
